question: How does ARC (Automatic Reference Counting) work in Swift?
answer:
ARC is a compile-time mechanism: the compiler inserts the retain and release calls, so an object is deallocated the instant its last strong reference goes away, with no collector and no pause.

• Strong (the default) — holds the object alive.
• `weak` — does not hold it, and the reference becomes nil automatically when the object is freed, which is why it must be a `var` Optional.
• `unowned` — does not hold it and is not Optional; reading it after the object is gone traps. Use it only when the referenced object is guaranteed to outlive this one.
• Closures capture strongly by default, and that is where most leaks come from. `[weak self]` in the capture list is the fix.
• Structs and enums are copied rather than reference-counted, so ARC does not apply to them — though a struct holding a class reference still participates through that property.

Because deallocation is deterministic, `deinit` is a reliable place to invalidate timers and cancel work, and a `print` in `deinit` is the cheapest leak test you have. The trade-off against a tracing collector is the mirror image: no pauses, but cycles are never collected, so you have to break them yourself.

question: What is a retain cycle? How do you detect and prevent them?
answer:
A retain cycle is two (or more) reference-counted objects holding strong references to each other so refcount never hits zero. The objects leak.

Common sources:
• Closures captured strongly by their owner (delegates, completion handlers, Combine sinks, NotificationCenter blocks).
• Bidirectional class relationships (parent ↔ child) without weak/unowned.
• Repeated NSTimer / DispatchSourceTimer holding `target = self`.

Detect:
• Xcode's Memory Graph Debugger — pause, click the icon, look for cycles (purple icons indicate leaks).
• Instruments → Leaks template.
• `deinit print` smoke test — does the object's `deinit` ever fire?

Fix: `[weak self]` capture lists, `weak` properties, invalidate timers in deinit.

question: How do you profile an iOS app with Instruments?
answer:
Instruments is Apple's profiler suite, attached to a running app from Xcode with Product → Profile.

Templates worth knowing:
• Time Profiler — sampled CPU stacks. Invert the call tree or filter to the main thread to find the method that is actually costing you.
• Allocations — memory over time. Find growth that never comes back down, and abandoned memory after a screen is dismissed.
• Leaks — objects with no path from a root, which in practice means retain cycles.
• Hangs — main-thread stalls over 250ms, reported with the stack that caused them.
• Animation Hitches — frames that missed their deadline, for UIKit and SwiftUI scrolling.
• Network and Energy Log — request timings and payload sizes, battery cost.
• App Launch — pre-main and post-main phases on one timeline.

Instrument your own code with `OSSignposter`, the Swift API that replaced the `os_signpost` C functions: your phases then appear as intervals alongside the system's tracks in any template.

Two rules that decide whether the numbers mean anything: profile a Release build on a real device, because the Simulator has your Mac's CPU and none of its thermal limits; and use MetricKit for real-user data, since `MXMetricPayload` reports launch time, hang rate, disk writes and battery from devices you will never hold.

question: How do you keep the main thread responsive in iOS apps?
answer:
The main thread draws every frame and handles every touch, so anything slow there is visible: over roughly 16ms you drop a frame, and over 250ms the system calls it a hang.

• Move work off with structured concurrency — `async let`, task groups, or an actor that owns the expensive state. Fan out independent requests instead of awaiting them one after another.
• Parse and decode off-main: a large JSON payload, image decoding, sorting or diffing a big collection. Hand only the finished value back to the UI.
• Never call synchronous I/O on the main thread: `Data(contentsOf:)`, directory enumeration, a Core Data fetch against a large store, or a `DispatchQueue.sync` onto a busy queue.
• Defer non-critical work until after the first frame — `viewDidAppear` or a `.task` — rather than doing it in `viewDidLoad`.
• Update the UI on the main actor only: annotate the type or the method `@MainActor` instead of sprinkling `DispatchQueue.main.async` calls.
• Since Swift 6.2 a module can default to main-actor isolation, which makes accidental main-thread work easier to write than before. Mark the functions that should leave the main actor `@concurrent`, or isolate them to an actor of their own.

Find the offenders with Instruments: the Hangs instrument surfaces the stalls directly, Time Profiler filtered to the main thread shows what was running, and the Main Thread Checker catches UIKit calls made off-main, which is the same bug in the other direction.

question: How do you optimize UITableView / UICollectionView scrolling performance?
answer:
Smooth scrolling means every frame's work fits in the frame budget: about 16ms at 60Hz, 8ms on a 120Hz ProMotion display.

• Cell reuse — dequeue, never construct per visible row, and cancel the in-flight image request in `prepareForReuse`.
• Prefetching — implement `UITableViewDataSourcePrefetching` / `UICollectionViewDataSourcePrefetching` so images and pages are fetched before the row is on screen, and cancel that work in the `cancelPrefetchingForRowsAt` callback.
• Pre-decode images off the main thread with `CGImageSourceCreateImageAtIndex` and `kCGImageSourceShouldCacheImmediately`, and downsample to the size you actually display instead of holding a full-resolution bitmap.
• Diffable data sources instead of `reloadData`, so only the changed rows are touched.
• Give a fast `estimatedRowHeight` (or `.estimated` in a compositional layout) so UIKit does not measure every row up front.
• Content configurations (`UIListContentConfiguration`) are cheaper than a custom cell carrying a dozen subviews.
• Avoid offscreen rendering: `cornerRadius` plus `clipsToBounds` on an opaque image view is cheap, a mask layer or a shadow without an explicit `shadowPath` is not.
• Do not call `layoutIfNeeded()` inside `cellForRowAt` — let the layout pass run once after configuration.

Profile before and after with Animation Hitches and Time Profiler; scrolling problems are usually one expensive call in cell configuration, not a hundred small ones.

question: How do you analyze and improve app launch time?
answer:
App launch splits into two measurable phases with different fixes: pre-main work done by dyld and the runtime, and everything from main until your first useful frame.

• Pre-main — dyld loading and linking your dylibs, Objective-C runtime setup, `+load` methods and static initialisers. Shrink it by cutting dynamic frameworks (each one costs dyld time), removing `+load`, and avoiding global values whose initialiser does real work.
• Post-main to first frame — `application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)`, scene setup, and building the first screen. This is where most of the avoidable time hides: SDK initialisation, a synchronous Keychain or Core Data hit, reading a config file, warming a cache.

Measure before you cut:
• Instruments' App Launch template shows both phases on one timeline.
• MetricKit's `MXAppLaunchMetric` gives a histogram of real users' cold launches, which is the only number that matters.
• `OSSignposter` intervals around your own startup phases show up alongside the system's tracks.

The reliable wins: defer every SDK that is not needed to draw the first screen, make services lazy so nothing initialises until first use, move cache warming into a background task started after the first frame, and merge small dynamic frameworks into fewer or into static ones.

Cold launch is the number to optimise — a warm launch reuses pages that are already resident and will flatter you.
